newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma renews ASEAN bid, faces U.N. rebuke.
newsitem.headline: Burma renews ASEAN bid, faces U.N. rebuke.

text.p: Burma's military government renewed efforts to join the ASEAN regional grouping on Thursday as its official media parried U.S. criticism and the United Nations issued another rebuke for its human rights record.

General Than Shwe, accompanied by military intelligence chief Lieutenant General Khin Nyunt and six members of the cabinet, arrived in Jakarta for a one-day summit meeting of the seven-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
Than Shwe said in a statement issued on his arrival that his visit "reaffirmed the sincere desire of the government and people of Myanmar (Burma) to integrate themselves into ASEAN".
He said he would use the summit "to renew personal contacts and exchange views with other heads of government".

While fellow observers Cambodia and Laos are on track to become full-fledged members of ASEAN next year, Burma's bid for membership is dogged by its crackdown on the pro-democracy movement led by Nobel peace laureate Aung San Suu Kyi.
Burma has detained and released nearly 1,000 NLD members or supporters in various crackdowns on the democracy movement since May.
The official media in Rangoon launched a fresh broadside against foreign criticism on Thursday, accusing the United States of trying to divide ASEAN over the Burma issue.

In reference to a Bangkok speech by President Bill Clinton singling out Burma for failing to recognise a democratically elected government, a commentary in all three state-run papers said the move was an "evil and dirty plot".
Using the word "Ngapwagyi" -- meaning "trouble maker" -- for the United States, the commentary said:

"It is an evil and dirty plot of Ngapwagyi, hitting the vulnerable spot to hinder Myanmar's wish to enter ASEAN and to make ASEAN nations become disunited. Ngapwagyi is implementing this scheme with all-out efforts".
In New York a key U.N. panel rebuked Burma for suppressing opposition, using forced labour to build its economy, torturing prisoners, abusing women and conducting summary executions.
In a resolution passed by consensus on Wednesday, the General Assembly's social, humanitarian and cultural committee said the government should protect and allow free access to Suu Kyi.
The decision by the committee, which includes all U.N. members, means an identical outcome when the Burma resolution comes before the General Assembly in the next two weeks.
At the suggestion of the Netherlands, the resolution also expressed alarm at an attack earlier this month on Suu Kyi's motorcade by a crowd pelting vehicles with stones.
The government denied it had anything to do with the attack but foreign diplomats in Burma had little doubt it was involved.

Burmese envoys said the resolution deliberately excluded any positive developments. It was far more intrusive than in the past and did not document improvements since 1990, such as an unprecedented period of peace and a rapidly growing economy.

ASEAN, which includes Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam, has been under pressure from Western nations and human rights activists to delay admitting Rangoon to the group because of the crackdown.
In the past month, cracks have appeared in ASEAN with some leaders publicly expressing reservations on allowing Burma to join Cambodia and Laos as full members in 1997.
But Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas told reporters on Wednesday that none of the ASEAN members opposed the entry of Burma.
Diplomatic sources said it was not a question of whether Burma would be admitted, but of when.
Burmese statistics show more than half of Burma's total foreign investment of $5.04 billion is from ASEAN members, with Singapore topping the list.
